raw_response:
I've been farming this same land in Quzhou for over forty years. My father farmed it before me. I know what this soil can do and what it can't. The North China Plain — this is wheat and corn country. That's what I grow. That's what I'll grow again this year. I have about 12 mu of flat, irrigated land, and I use all of it.

Come October I'll plant winter wheat. I always use the improved variety from the county seed station — not the old traditional seed, because yields are better, and my son says I should keep up. But I'm not going to try some new hybrid I've never heard of either. I'll apply compound fertilizer at planting and come back with urea when the wheat is jointing in spring. Water here is our main worry — we pump from the well. I'll irrigate three times: before the ground freezes, at jointing, and at heading. Maybe not the fourth time some people do at grain fill, because the water table keeps dropping and it's expensive. Two or three rounds of pesticide — herbicide in autumn, then something for rust and aphids in spring if I see it.

After wheat harvest in June, I'll plant summer maize right away on the same 12 mu — basically no-till, I just run the rotary over it lightly to break up the straw. Hybrid seed, that's all anyone plants now. The maize grows fast in the summer heat. I give it fertilizer at planting and a topdressing when it's knee-high. Usually one irrigation if the rains don't come. Spray herbicide once, maybe spray for corn borer if it's a bad year.

That's it. No vegetables, no cash crops. I'm 65, my knees aren't what they were. Wheat and maize I can mostly manage with the small tractor my son and I share. The price isn't always great but it's stable, and the government still subsidizes the seeds and fertilizer a little.
